title: Clare to Agnes
hookLine: Clare writes to a king's daughter turned nun: gaze into Christ as into a mirror
tomorrow: if you could ask God for anything, what would you ask?

lines: A KING'S DAUGHTER, A POOR NUN.
cards: A phone's front camera can flip the picture, so the face on the screen isn't quite the one other people see. Selfies get retaken, filtered, deleted. Clare of Assisi has a mirror puzzle stranger than any filter.
She's writing to Agnes, the daughter of the king of Bohemia, who, Clare's first letter says, could have married an emperor and chose to be a poor nun instead.
And Clare tells her: gaze into that mirror every day, and keep studying your face in it. The mirror is Christ. So how do you find your own face in someone else's?

teach.b: Clare solves it in her fourth letter by walking Agnes across the mirror. She calls Christ a mirror without a stain. At its edge, poverty: the child laid in a manger, wrapped in swaddling clothes.
Across its surface, humility: the long, ordinary labor of someone who served.
And in its depth, love beyond words: Christ on the cross.
In another letter she gives a small ladder of verbs: gaze, consider, contemplate, desiring to imitate. First you look. Then you think about what you see.
Then you rest in it. Then you want to become it. It's the slow way of looking, the opposite of a scroll.
An ordinary mirror shows you yourself as you are. Clare's shows you Christ, and then asks you to study your own face in him: where it already looks like his, and where it doesn't yet.
The mirror isn't for judging how you look. It's for seeing who you're becoming. She wants Agnes to put on that same beauty, and she means poverty, humility and love.
And here's the one to tell a friend: Clare writes all this to a king's daughter with delight, not as a scolding. She isn't telling a princess to feel small. She's telling her where the beauty is.

how: Poor Clare nuns and other Franciscans read Clare's letters to Agnes for prayer, and her ladder of gaze, consider, contemplate is used as a way of praying with an image of Christ.

o: Clare's letters on gazing at Christ as a mirror
a princess's letters asking Clare for money

s: Clare's mirror is about looking hard at yourself
the popular reading. the mirror is Christ, and Agnes studies her own face in him.
Clare wrote to a king's daughter who chose to become a nun
her first letter says Agnes could have married an emperor.
Clare's letters scold Agnes for having been royal
she writes with delight, telling her where real beauty is.

games.q: your little brother copies a streamer's every move, the minute he sees it. by Clare's ladder, what's he skipping?
o: nothing; imitating is the whole ladder.
looking only at himself instead of anyone.
gazing, considering and resting before imitating.
games.why: Clare's ladder ends in desiring to imitate, but it starts with gaze, consider, contemplate. you look, think, and rest before you become.

practice: If there's a mirror nearby, sit where you can see your face; if not, recall it. No retakes. Look gently, then let your attention move with Clare, from your face to the manger, the ordinary work, the cross.
If you pray, follow her verbs slowly through the sit: gaze, consider, contemplate.

wordCard.voice: Clare to Agnes. Clare of Assisi's letters to a king's daughter turned nun, built around a mirror that is Christ.

orig.note: Latin for mirror; Clare wrote her letters in Latin.

carryVoice: Keep this: gaze into the mirror, and look for his face in yours. Until tomorrow.
